turns.text:
# **Auxiliary variables and missingness in NHANES lipids:** what is known

The papers retrieved provide general guidance on auxiliary-variable choice and NHANES-style missingness, but none directly analyze predictors of missingness in the NHANES lipid panel or give a ready-made auxiliary-variable set for fasting-subsample lipids. The answer therefore focuses on principles and related NHANES work that can guide your own variable selection.

## **Missingness patterns in NHANES‑like data**

- In NHANES, subsample designs (e.g., fasting subsamples) create **block-like patterns of missingness** rather than item-by-item gaps, and these blocks are associated with survival and other outcomes, implying non-ignorable missingness if ignored  (Frölich et al., 2024; Pridham et al., 2022; Chauhan et al., 2023).  
- Analyses of NHANES and similar surveys show that missingness in health variables can depend on demographics, health behaviors, and clinical indicators (e.g., BMI, smoking, exercise, comorbidities), which are used as predictors in imputation models  (Pan & Chen, 2023; Pridham et al., 2022; Blazek et al., 2020).

### Typical predictors used in NHANES imputation case studies

| Variable type                | Examples used as predictors | Citations |
|-----------------------------|-----------------------------|----------|
| Demographics                | Age, sex, race/ethnicity, education, income, marital status |  (Pan & Chen, 2023; Blazek et al., 2020)|
| Health status / comorbidity | General health, hypertension, kidney disease, cardiovascular disease |  (Pan & Chen, 2023; Blazek et al., 2020)|
| Behaviors                   | Smoking, alcohol, physical activity, diet quality |  (Pan & Chen, 2023; Chauhan et al., 2023)|
| Anthropometrics / labs      | BMI, blood pressure, hsCRP, “overweight” status |  (Pan & Chen, 2023; Chauhan et al., 2023)|

**Figure 1:** Common NHANES-style predictors used in imputation models

## **How to choose auxiliary variables for lipid-panel MI**

**Prioritize variables that predict the lipid values, not just missingness**

- Theory and simulations show that including auxiliary variables that **only predict missingness but not the lipid itself** can **increase bias** when data are MNAR, especially when missingness is driven by the outcome or both outcome and exposure  (Curnow et al., 2024; Mainzer et al., 2024; Curnow et al., 2023).  
- Recommended strategy: include **variables most predictive of the partially observed variable** (here LDL, HDL, TG, total cholesterol) plus all variables in the analysis model  (Curnow et al., 2024; Mainzer et al., 2024; Madley-Dowd et al., 2023; Hardt et al., 2012).

**Avoid problematic auxiliary variables**

- Too many weakly correlated auxiliaries, especially in small samples, can produce **downward bias and reduced precision**; a rough rule-of-thumb is not to let the variables-to-complete-cases ratio fall below about 1:3  (Hardt et al., 2012).  
- Auxiliary variables that act as **colliders** (share a cause with both lipid level and its missingness) may induce bias and higher SEs and should be excluded where plausible  (Curnow et al., 2023).  

## **Role of missingness indicators and advanced MI strategies**

- Including **missingness indicators** in MI models can sometimes reduce bias when missingness is informative and MNAR, particularly when missingness depends on the variable itself, but can also increase bias with unmeasured confounding  (Sperrin & Martin, 2020; Mainzer et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024).  
- NHANES-based and other public-health simulations show that flexible imputation engines (e.g., MICE with CART and carefully chosen auxiliaries) can handle complex block missingness and improve prediction and bias over default models  (Pridham et al., 2022; Chauhan et al., 2023).

## **Conclusion**

No paper directly lists predictors of fasting-subsample missingness for NHANES lipids or a canonical auxiliary-variable set. Evidence supports: (1) modeling block missingness using rich demographic, behavioral, and clinical predictors; (2) prioritizing variables that strongly predict the lipid measures themselves; and (3) avoiding variables that only predict missingness, are colliders, or are numerous but weakly related, to limit bias and instability in multiple imputation.

## **Reported missingness of lipid variables in NHANES**

The included papers largely analyze NHANES lipid data but almost never report detailed **percent missingness by lipid variable**. Only one paper provides explicit overall missingness percentages for standard lipids.

## **Explicitly reported missingness**

### Overall lipid-panel missingness in NHANES 1999–2018

Gao et al. (US trends in cholesterol screening and lipids) report, for their NHANES analytic sample (1999–2018)  (Gao et al., 2023):

| Measure / variable group                 | Percent missing | Citations |
|-----------------------------------------|-----------------|-----------|
| Cholesterol screening (self-report)     | 3.0%            |  (Gao et al., 2023)|
| Total cholesterol (TC) + HDL-C          | 6.2%            |  (Gao et al., 2023)|
| Triglycerides (TG) + LDL-C              | 6.8%            |  (Gao et al., 2023)|
| Lipid‑lowering medication use           | 0.1%            |  (Gao et al., 2023)|

**Figure 1:** Reported missingness for NHANES lipid variables

These percentages are for the combined 1999–2018 cycles and reflect the share of participants with missing data on each outcome in that specific analysis, not official NHANES-wide missingness rates.

## **Information from other NHANES lipid analyses**

Other NHANES-based studies state that participants lacking specific lipid values or lipid data were **excluded**, but they do not quantify percent missingness for each lipid variable:

- Li et al. (NHANES 2007–2018) excluded participants “with missing lipid values” but did not report percentages  (Li et al., 2022).  
- Sun et al. (NHANES 1999–2018) give counts of participants without TC, TG, and LDL-C data but not proportions relative to the full eligible sample  (Sun et al., 2022).  
- Several additional NHANES analyses (e.g., dyslipidemia, TC/HDL ratio, sarcopenia, environmental exposures) either require **complete lipid data** or mention excluding those with missing lipids, without reporting explicit missingness percentages  (Huang et al., 2024; Zheng et al., 2024; Huang et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2022).

## **Conclusion**

Within these abstracts and excerpts, the only quantified missingness for NHANES lipid variables is from Gao et al.: about 6–7% missing for TC/HDL-C and TG/LDL-C in their 1999–2018 analysis. Other NHANES lipid studies acknowledge excluding participants with missing lipid values but do not provide corresponding percent-missingness figures for LDL, TG, HDL, or total cholesterol.

back to the consensus search: Save this verbatim: ## **Reported Missingness in NHANES Variables: What Is Available?**

Research using NHANES often discusses missing data, but very few papers actually publish full “percent missing by variable” tables. The available work gives only fragmentary percentages for specific domains or ranges.

### **How Often Is Percent Missingness Reported?**

- In a review of 37 NHANES-based dissertations and 17 subsequent articles (2007–2017), **only 9 studies reported missing-data percentages for key variables**, and **only 1 journal article** did so  (Yu et al., 2023).  
- Where reported, **7 of 9 studies had ≤10% missingness** on key variables, and **2 had >10%**  (Yu et al., 2023).  
- NHANES program guidance recommends using multiple imputation or adjusted weights when a variable has **>10% missing data**  (Yu et al., 2023; Roberts & English, 2016).

### **Examples of Reported Percent Missingness**

| Context / Variable set                            | Reported missingness range | Citations |
|---------------------------------------------------|----------------------------|-----------|
| SEM variables (food security, cotinine, depression) | 0.0%–25.3%                 |  (Hartwell et al., 2019)|
| Self‑reported conditions over 10 NHANES cycles    | 0%–97% (varies by item/cycle) |  (Siontis & Patel, 2024)|
| DXA (body composition) exam data 1999–2004        | ~21% of eligible participants missing in whole or part |  (Schenker et al., 2011; Qin et al., 2009)|
| DXA fat measure (DXDTOPF) in an example analysis  | ~20% missing               |  (Qin et al., 2009)|
| Child systolic BP (SBP) in 2017–2018 NHANES       | 44% missing (by design plus measurement gaps) |  (Zivich et al., 2025)|
| Lead-surveillance predictors (e.g., age of housing, poverty) | Up to ~35% missing for key predictors |  (Roberts & English, 2016)|
| 2015–2016 questionnaire items (many blocks)       | Average missingness rate ≈ 62%, SD ≈ 38%, with some questions “extremely low” response (e.g., income) |  (Mao et al., 2019)|

**Figure 1:** Illustrative ranges of missingness for selected NHANES variable groups

### **Patterns and Mechanisms**

- Missingness often shows **block or “swiss-cheese” patterns** by questionnaire module or exam component  (Pridham et al., 2022; Mao et al., 2019; Chauhan et al., 2023).  
- Some variables are **missing at random (MAR)** with respect to race/ethnicity or other covariates (e.g., food security more often missing in Mexican American and other Hispanic groups)  (Hartwell et al., 2019).  
- For several components (DXA, child lead, BP), missingness is **not completely at random** and is related to age, BMI, or design decisions, implying potential bias if ignored  (Pridham et al., 2022; Schenker et al., 2011; Zivich et al., 2025; Roberts & English, 2016; Qin et al., 2009).

## **Conclusion**

There is no single published, comprehensive table of “percent missingness of all NHANES variables.” Existing studies report missingness only for specific variables or domains, with percentages ranging from near 0% to >90% depending on item and cycle. For precise percent-missing values, analysts typically must compute missingness directly from the NHANES files for the specific variables and cycles of interest.
